Empirical Research Plan: “Graduation” Programs in Six Countries  
--------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------
Strategy: Difference-in-Differences (DiD) with household (or village) fixed effects, complemented by an event-study specification.  

Rationale  
• The intervention was **randomly assigned** within each site (either at household- or cluster-level) and we observe households **before treatment (baseline) and twice after treatment**.  
• A DiD estimator removes time-invariant unobservables and controls for common shocks; the event-study lets us trace dynamics (short- vs. medium-run).  
• Random assignment plus a rich baseline makes DiD assumptions highly plausible and transparent to test (e.g., pre-trend balance, attrition).  
Other methods (RDD, IV) are not natural fits because there is no running variable and no obvious instrument beyond the random assignment itself.

2. Treatment and Control
------------------------
Treatment variable  
• Treat_i = 1 if household i was assigned to receive the full Graduation package in its site; 0 otherwise.

Control group  
• Households in the same sampling frame that were **randomly assigned to delayed or no program** status serve as counterfactual. Ideally they reside in different hamlets/clusters to minimise spillovers; if randomisation was at village level we include untreated villages only.

Timing  
• t = 0 : Baseline survey (pre-intervention).  
• t = 1 : Endline 1 (~24 months, immediately after program completion).  
• t = 2 : Endline 2 (~36 months, ~12 months post-completion).  
Event date is the month of productive-asset transfer (close to programme start); we normalise survey dates to “months since transfer”.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of the program, outcomes in treatment and control would have evolved similarly.  
• Plausibility: Random assignment strengthens it; we can formally test using any pre-program outcomes (e.g., retrospective shocks, pre-baseline wages) and site-specific time trends.

A2. No spillovers/SUTVA: Control households are not indirectly treated.  
• Plausibility: Possible within-village spillovers (role-model effects, labour-market equilibrium). We will cluster at the randomisation level, include village fixed effects, and test for distance-related contamination where GPS is available.

A3. Stable composition: Attrition is not correlated with treatment once we condition on observables.  
• Plausibility: Three-wave panel allows checks; we will implement Lee (2009) bounds and inverse-probability weighting.

A4. Treatment fidelity: Treated households actually receive the intended bundle, and controls do not.  
• Plausibility: Implementation reports and monitoring data exist; we can instrument with assignment if some non-compliance occurred (first-stage > 0.8 in other studies).

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation
-------------------------------------------
T1. Differential attrition  
• Mitigation: Compare attrition rates & baseline covariates by arm, run Lee bounds, IPW, and worst-case Imbens-Manski bounds.

T2. Spillovers / general-equilibrium effects  
• Mitigation: Include geographically lagged treatment share; re-estimate excluding controls within X km of treated clusters; cluster SEs at village; present “as-treated vs pure controls” subsample.

T3. Heterogeneous roll-out timing across sites  
• Mitigation: Include site-by-wave fixed effects; estimate within-site DiD and meta-analyse site-specific treatment effects with random-effects weights.

5. R Code Outline
-----------------
```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)     # fast high-dim FE
library(ggplot2)
library(modelsummary)

# 1. Load & merge three survey rounds
base  <- fread("graduation_baseline.csv")
end1  <- fread("graduation_endline1.csv")
end2  <- fread("graduation_endline2.csv")

# Harmonise and stack
for(dt in list(base,end1,end2)){
  dt[,wave := fifelse(.SD==base,"t0",
                fifelse(.SD==end1,"t1","t2"))]
}

panel <- rbindlist(list(base,end1,end2), use.names=TRUE, fill=TRUE)

# 2. Key variables
panel[, treat  := as.integer(treatment_assignment==1)]       # intent-to-treat
panel[, post1  := (wave=="t1")]
panel[, post2  := (wave=="t2")]
panel[, post   := 1*(wave!="t0")]

# Outcomes (example: real monthly per-capita consumption)
panel[, cons_pc := total_consumption/household_size / cpi_adj]

# 3. Main DiD (pooled waves)
did_main <- feols(cons_pc ~ treat*post | hh_id + wave + site, 
                  data = panel, cluster = "cluster_id")
etable(did_main, se="cluster")

# 4. Event-study: month_relative = months since transfer
panel[, rel_month := survey_month - asset_transfer_month]
event <- feols(cons_pc ~ i(rel_month, treat, ref=-1) | hh_id + site + survey_month, 
               data=panel, cluster="cluster_id")
iplot(event, xlab="Months since transfer", ylab="Δ consumption")

# 5. Robustness: Lee bounds for attrition
library(LeeBounds)
lee <- lee_bounds(Y="cons_pc", D="treat", R="responded", data=panel[wave=="t2"])
print(lee)
```

6. Expected Results
-------------------
Theory (big-push + relaxing multiple constraints) predicts **positive and sustained** effects.  
• Direction: Treated households will exhibit higher per-capita consumption, productive assets, and subjective well-being at both t1 and t2.  
• Magnitude (benchmarking BRAC 2002): +5–10 % in consumption at t1, persisting at +4–8 % at t2; asset values +30 %; self-employment income +30–40 %.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DiD)
-------------------------------------------
C1: Parallel pre-trends tested and satisfied – 1  
C2: No differential attrition – 0.5 (needs Lee/IPW)  
C3: No spillovers – 0.5 (plausible but not guaranteed)  
C4: Correct treatment timing and common shocks controlled – 1  
C5: Appropriate clustering and inference – 1  

Total ≈ 4/5 → Good overall credibility.
